title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
In this exercise, we will recreate an ONS labour market estimate published online in the table EMP07 Temporary Employees. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey (QLFS).
Learning outcomes:

To become more familiar with QLFS datasets.
To become familiar with producing weighted population estimates
To understand how some ONS estimates are produced



The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



One you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible, for example in a folder named LFS_exercises. We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that are are going to need…

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

… And open the QLFS dataset:

## setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")


# Import  the data from a Stata format dataset
lfs_od24 <- read_dta("Data/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta")

Inspect the dataset and find out the number of cases and variables.

ncol(lfs_od24) # Number of columns

[1] 803

nrow(lfs_od24) # Number of rows (observations)

[1] 63069



Revision questionAnswers


How many variables are there?


There are 803 variables in the dataset.



As there are many variables in the dataset, let’s create a copy with just the variables we will use. We can also use this opportunity to make the variable categories easier to understand by converting them into factors. For greater clarity, we also remove unused categories of categorical variables using droplevels().

mydata <- lfs_od24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PWT24, JBTP101, FTPT, INECAC05, JOBTYP, SEX)|>
  mutate(across(.cols=JBTP101:SEX, 
                .fns=as_factor,"both")
         )|>
  droplevels()

QuestionsAnswers



How many cases are there?
What does the variable INECAC05 relate to?
Why are there many missing cases on the variables: JBTP101, FTPT and JOBTYP.




There are 63,069 cases
INECAC05 records NULL
Respondents not in employment are coded as missing values for these variables. Missing values were recorded as -9 “Does not apply” and -8 “No answer” in the original data.







In order to provide reliable estimates of population values, survey data needs to be weighted when analysed. Weights are variables whose values increase or decrease the relative importance of observations, depending on how likely respondents were to take part to the survey. Some weights are only designed to correct the relative importance of observations, whereas others in addition also enable calculating population totals - the latter are called grossing weights.
Below, we compare weighted and unweighted frequencies and percentages.
We will be using as_survey_design(), a R function from the survey and srvyr packages that in effect creates a weighted version of our data.
Let us first examine the variable measuring - JOBTYP - whether respondents work in a temporary job or not:

table(mydata$JOBTYP)


          [-9] Does not apply                [-8] No answer 
                        36698                            15 
                [1] Permanent [2] Not permanent in some way 
                        25104                          1252 

round(100*prop.table(table(mydata$JOBTYP)),1)


          [-9] Does not apply                [-8] No answer 
                         58.2                           0.0 
                [1] Permanent [2] Not permanent in some way 
                         39.8                           2.0 


… and create a version without missing values.

mydata <- mydata |> 
          mutate (
                 JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[2] Not permanent in some way",
                                 "Temporary",
                                  "Not temporary"),
                 JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[-9] Does not apply" | 
                                  JOBTYP == "[-8] No answer",
                                  NA,
                                  JobTmp),
                 JobTmp = as.factor(JobTmp)
                  )

table(mydata$JobTmp)


Not temporary     Temporary 
        25104          1252 


Using a function from the survey package, we create a weights-aware version of the data that we will be using for susbsequent analysis:

mydata.s<-mydata|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

Please note that we needed to remove observations with missing weights values, in effect observations that should not be taken into account to calculate population values. If we don’t we will get an error message.
We can now compute weighted frequencies and percentages using a survey specific command: svytable():

svytable(~JobTmp, mydata.s)

JobTmp
Not temporary     Temporary 
     27802100       1514206 

round(100*
       prop.table(
         svytable(~JobTmp, mydata.s)
         ),1
      )

JobTmp
Not temporary     Temporary 
         94.8           5.2 





QuestionsAnswers



Do the frequencies change noticeably when the weight is applied?
Create a variable to indicate those working part time and examine weighted and unweighted frequencies.




PWT24 is a grossing weight. Therefore, frequencies now reflect population totals.
The syntax below computes a variable recording whether respondents work part-time or not and produce weighted frequency tables.


 mydata <- mydata |> 
                  mutate (
                    PartTime = ifelse(FTPT == "[4] New Deal-PT" | FTPT  == "[2] Part time",
                                      "Part-time",
                                      "Not part-time"),
                   PartTime = ifelse(FTPT == "[-9] Does not apply" | FTPT == "[-8] No answer",
                                      NA,
                                      PartTime),

                    PartTime = as.factor(PartTime)
                  )


mydata.s<-mydata|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

round(100*
       prop.table(
         table(mydata$PartTime)
         ),1
      )


Not part-time     Part-time 
         73.1          26.9 

round(100*
       prop.table(
         svytable(~PartTime, mydata.s)
         ),1
      )

PartTime
Not part-time     Part-time 
         75.2          24.8 









We then obtain the percentages of full-time and part-time employees by job tenure, by creating a contingency table:

t1<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp,mydata.s)

t1

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time      21736784    700619
  Part-time           6060549    812464

            round(
                  100*prop.table(
                   t1
                   ,1) # Requests denominators to be each working time status
                  ,1)

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          96.9       3.1
  Part-time              88.2      11.8


We can add a third variable to the table to simultaneously examine the number of temporary and part-time employees by gender.

t2<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp+SEX,mydata.s)

            round(
                  100*prop.table(
                   t2
                   ,3) # Requests denominators to be each gender/working time combination.
                  ,1)

, , SEX = [1] Male

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          85.0       2.7
  Part-time              10.1       2.3

, , SEX = [2] Female

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          63.5       2.1
  Part-time              31.2       3.2





QuestionsAnswers



How many people are temporary employees (all and part-time) in this quarter?
How many females are in part-time temporary employment?
How many applicable cases to we have for the above analysis?




There are 1,514,206 temporary employees.
There are 475,513 females in part-time temporary employment
In order to get the number of valid cases, we need to look at unweighted frequencies. The number of (unweighted) valid cases for this analysis is 26,351




Note: You can check if your results match those in the ONS EMP07 dataset.

title: Exercise 3: Labour Market Flows
text:
The exercise presents three different methods for examining labour market flows - ie the transitions between one kind of involvement in paid work (for example, full-time employed) to another one (for example, economically inactive) using longitudinal data from the Labour Force Survey.
The estimates in this exercise relate to figures published by ONS on the ‘Labour market flows NSA’ sheet in Table X02. NSA stands for ‘non seasonally adjusted’, as we will be examining flows that took place between two quarters (as opposed to seasonally adjusted yearly averages).
Learning outcomes:

Becoming familiar with Two Quarter Longitudinal Labour Force Survey data
Being able to estimate labour market flows using different methods
Being able to use longitudinal weights



This exercise relies on the Two-Quarter LFS Longitudinal Dataset for July - December 2024, which is available from the UK Data Service (Study number 9348).




library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

Let’s open the dataset. As in the previous exercises, we downloaded it into a Data folder inside the working directory: LFS_exercises.

        "Data/UKDA-9348-stata/stata/stata13/lgwt24_2q_js24_od24_eul.dta"
                    )
# ... And create a smaller, easier to handle,  data frame

title: Weekly earnings of employees
text:
In this exercise, you will recreate a labour market analysis by the ONS, reported in the table EARN04: Gross weekly earnings of full-time employees [last accessed 21/02/2025]. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using data from the Quarterly Labour Force Survey.
Learning outcomes:

To understand better how ONS earnings statistics are produced
To become more familiar with key variables from the QLFS
To learn using income weights appropriately



The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



We will assume that the working directory for this exercise - where syntax files and other materials will be located - will be a folder named LFS_exercises. Once you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible inside LFS_exercises, for example in another folder named Data.
We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that are are going to need:

title: Understanding Confidence Intervals with UK LFS Data
text:
Introduction
In statistical analysis, a confidence interval serves as a crucial tool for estimating population parameters based on sample data. It provides a range of values within which the true population parameter is likely to lie, along with a specified level of confidence, typically expressed as a percentage such as 95% [1, 2]. This range quantifies the uncertainty inherent in estimates derived from a sample, offering more information than a single point estimate [2, 3]. For instance, a 95% confidence interval suggests that if the same population were sampled repeatedly and confidence intervals calculated for each sample, approximately 95% of these intervals would contain the true population parameter [4, 5]. It is important to understand that a confidence interval does not provide the probability that a specific calculated interval contains the true parameter, but rather reflects the reliability of the estimation process over many repeated samples [6, 7]. The width of a confidence interval is indicative of the precision of the estimate; a narrower interval suggests a more stable and precise estimate, while a wider interval implies greater variability and less certainty about the true value [1, 5]. Understanding and interpreting confidence intervals is fundamental for drawing meaningful conclusions about a population from a sample.
This worksheet will focus on utilizing the UK Quarterly Labour Force Survey (LFS) October-December 2023 dataset, which we will refer to as od23, to illustrate the practical application of confidence intervals. The LFS is a comprehensive survey of households in the UK, providing extensive data on the labour market, including employment, unemployment, economic inactivity, and various related topics [8, 9]. Conducted quarterly, the LFS employs a complex sampling design to ensure national representativeness [10, 11]. The October-December 2023 dataset captures a specific snapshot of the UK labour market during that period [User Query]. While the LFS generally boasts a large sample size, which contributes to relatively small sampling errors, it is worth noting that recent periods have experienced challenges with falling response rates [11, 12, 13]. This context is important for users to bear in mind when interpreting the results derived from this dataset.
The primary objective of this worksheet is to guide users through the process of calculating and interpreting confidence intervals for key labour market indicators using the od23 dataset. We will explore three distinct exercises, each focusing on a different aspect of working with confidence intervals in the context of survey data. These exercises will cover the comparison of weighted and unweighted estimates, the comparison of confidence intervals across different subgroups, and the adjustment of confidence intervals based on survey design effects. By working through these exercises, users will gain practical experience in analyzing survey data and understanding the nuances of confidence interval estimation.
Exercise 1: Comparing Weighted and Unweighted Estimates of Mean Gross Weekly Earnings
Survey weights play a critical role in the analysis of survey data, particularly when the sample is not a simple random sample of the population. These weights are applied to individual responses to ensure that the sample data accurately reflects the characteristics of the target population [14, 15]. In the case of the UK LFS, weights are used to account for the survey’s complex multi-stage stratified random sampling design, as well as to adjust for potential biases arising from non-response [11, 16, 17]. The October-December 2023 dataset includes the person-level weight variable PIWT24 [8]. Utilizing these weights is essential for obtaining estimates that are representative of the UK population as a whole. In contrast, estimates calculated without applying survey weights, known as unweighted estimates, can be biased and may not accurately reflect the true population parameters [General statistical knowledge]. This is because certain demographic groups might be over- or underrepresented in the sample due to the sampling process or differences in response rates. Therefore, comparing weighted and unweighted estimates can highlight the importance of accounting for the survey design in statistical analysis.
To illustrate this, we will examine the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) from the od23 dataset. We will first calculate the unweighted mean and its 95% confidence interval. Then, we will create a survey design object in R, incorporating the PIWT24 weight, and use this object to calculate the weighted mean and its corresponding 95% confidence interval [15, 18, 19, 20].
R Syntax:
First, ensure that you have the necessary R packages installed. You will likely need dplyr for data manipulation and survey for handling complex survey designs.
```R # Install necessary packages if you haven’t already # install.packages(“dplyr”) # install.packages(“survey”)

Load the packages
library(dplyr) library(survey)


Assuming your dataset ‘od23’ is loaded into R


For example:


od23 <- read.csv(“path/to/your/od23.csv”)


1. Calculate unweighted mean and 95% confidence interval for GRSSWK
unweighted_mean <- mean(od23\(GRSSWK, na.rm = TRUE)
unweighted_sd <- sd(od23\)GRSSWK, na.rm = TRUE) n <- sum(!is.na(od23$GRSSWK)) unweighted_se <- unweighted_sd / sqrt(n) unweighted_ci_lower <- unweighted_mean - 1.96 * unweighted_se unweighted_ci_upper <- unweighted_mean + 1.96 * unweighted_se
cat(“Unweighted Mean Gross Weekly Earnings:”, unweighted_mean, “”) cat(“Unweighted 95% Confidence Interval:”, unweighted_ci_lower, “to”, unweighted_ci_upper, “”)


2. Create a survey design object using PIWT24 weight
design_od23 <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = od23)


3. Calculate weighted mean and 95% confidence interval for GRSSWK
weighted_mean <- svymean(~GRSSWK, design = design_od23, na.rm = TRUE) weighted_ci <- confint(weighted_mean)
cat(“Weighted Mean Gross Weekly Earnings:”, coef(weighted_mean), “”) cat(“Weighted 95% Confidence Interval:”, weighted_ci[1], “to”, weighted_ci[2], “”)

This worksheet will guide you through working with confidence intervals (CIs) using the UK Quarterly Labour Force Survey (LFS) October-December 2023 data (od24). You will learn how to compare weighted and unweighted estimates, compare weighted CIs across regions, and adjust CIs using design effects.




In survey data, weighting is often used to ensure that estimates are representative of the population. Here, we compare the weighted and unweighted estimates of mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals. The weighting variable is PIWT24.




# Load necessary libraries
library(survey)
library(dplyr)
library(haven)

od24 <- read_dta(
        "~/Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
                    )

# Calculate unweighted mean and CI
unweighted_mean <- mean(od24$GRSSWK, na.rm = TRUE)
unweighted_ci <- t.test(od24$GRSSWK)$conf.int

# Create survey design object
lfs_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = od24)

# Calculate weighted mean and CI
weighted_mean <- svymean(~GRSSWK, design = lfs_design, na.rm = TRUE)
weighted_ci <- confint(weighted_mean)





# Print results
cat("Unweighted Mean:", unweighted_mean, "\n")

Unweighted Mean: 75.80171 

cat("Unweighted CI:", unweighted_ci, "\n")

Unweighted CI: 73.33218 78.27124 

cat("Weighted Mean:", weighted_mean, "\n")

Weighted Mean: 693.7501 

cat("Weighted CI:", weighted_ci, "\n")

Weighted CI: 681.8465 705.6538 





The unweighted mean and CI do not account for the survey design, while the weighted mean and CI use the weighting variable PIWT24 to produce representative estimates. The weighted CI is typically wider due to the incorporation of design effects.




Why is the weighted CI wider than the unweighted CI?
What does the weighting variable PIWT24 represent?
How might ignoring weights affect the interpretation of the results?





The weighted CI is wider because it accounts for the survey design, including stratification and clustering, which increases the variability of the estimate.
PIWT24 is the person-level weight for the survey, ensuring the sample represents the population.
Ignoring weights can lead to biased estimates that do not reflect the true population parameters.








In this exercise, we compare the weighted confidence intervals of the proportion of female employees who self-reported working part-time (FTPT) in London and the North West. The regional variable is GOVTOF2.




# Filter data for females and part-time workers
female_parttime <- od24 %>% filter(SEX == 2 & FTPT == 2)

# Create survey design object
lfs_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = female_parttime)

# Calculate weighted proportions and CIs for London and North West
london_prop <- svymean(~GOVTOF2 == 7, design = lfs_design)
northwest_prop <- svymean(~GOVTOF2 == 2, design = lfs_design)

london_ci <- confint(london_prop)
northwest_ci <- confint(northwest_prop)





# Print results
cat("London Proportion:", london_prop, "\n")

London Proportion: 0.9089568 0.09104316 

cat("London CI:", london_ci, "\n")

London CI: 0.8916423 0.07372865 0.9262713 0.1083577 

cat("North West Proportion:", northwest_prop, "\n")

North West Proportion: 0.8962006 0.1037994 

cat("North West CI:", northwest_ci, "\n")

North West CI: 0.8774707 0.08506962 0.9149304 0.1225293 





The weighted proportions and CIs show the estimated proportion of female part-time workers in London and the North West. The CIs provide a range within which the true proportion is likely to lie.




What does the overlap (or lack thereof) between the CIs for London and the North West indicate?
How does the sample size in each region affect the width of the CI?
Why is it important to use weights when comparing regions?





Overlapping CIs suggest no statistically significant difference between the proportions, while non-overlapping CIs indicate a significant difference.
Larger sample sizes result in narrower CIs, as they provide more precise estimates.
Weights ensure that the estimates are representative of the population in each region, accounting for differences in sampling probabilities.








Design effects account for the impact of survey design (e.g., clustering and stratification) on the precision of estimates. Here, we adjust the CI of the proportion of people in employment (ILODEFR) by age bands (AGE) using design effects published in Volume 1 of the LFS documentation.




# Load design effects for age bands
design_effects <- c(1.2, 1.5, 1.8) # Example values for age bands 16-24, 25-34, 35+

# Create survey design object
lfs_design <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~PIWT24, data = od24)

# Calculate weighted proportions and CIs by age band
age_props <- svyby(~ILODEFR == 1, ~AGE, design = lfs_design, svymean)

# Adjust CIs using design effects
adjusted_cis <- confint(age_props) * sqrt(design_effects)












The adjusted CIs account for the design effects, which increase the width of the CIs to reflect the reduced precision due to the survey design. This provides a more accurate measure of uncertainty.




What is a design effect, and why is it important?
How do design effects impact the width of the CI?
Why might design effects vary across age bands?





A design effect measures how much the survey design increases the variance of an estimate compared to a simple random sample. It is important because it ensures accurate uncertainty estimates.
Design effects increase the width of the CI, reflecting the reduced precision due to clustering and stratification.
Design effects vary across age bands due to differences in sample sizes, clustering, and stratification within each age group.






This worksheet has introduced you to working with confidence intervals in survey data, including weighting, regional comparisons, and design effects. Apply these techniques to your own analyses to ensure accurate and representative results. ```

title: Exercise 4:  Estimate precision and uncertainty
text:
This series of exercises focuses on the precision of estimates calculated from Labour Force Survey data, in other words the degree to which we can trust them to reflect the likely values in the population. In order to do this, we will compute similar measures as before - means and proportions but this time we will be focusing on their confidence intervals.
Learning objectives:

To be able to compute and interpret confidence intervals of earnings in the LFS;
To be able to assess the impact of weighting on weighting ;
To be able to interpret CIs for regional differences;
To be able to use published LFS design effects and apply them to your own estimates;



In this exercise we will be using Quarterly LFS data for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



We will assume that the working directory for this exercise - where syntax files and other materials will be located - will be a folder named LFS_exercises. Once you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible inside LFS_exercises for example in a folder called `Data.
We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that we are going to need:

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

Let’s open the dataset.

## setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")

### Importing a Stata format dataset
lfs_od24 <- read_dta(
        "Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
                    )

To make data manipulation easier, let’s create a data frame with just the variables we need for the exercise. We can also use this opportunity to convert categorical variables into factors in order to make them easier to understand.

dataex4 <- lfs_od24 |>
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,
         FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX,INDE07M,GOVTOF2 ) |>
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05:GOVTOF2),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()




In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for earnings: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine gross weekly earnings and compute its unweighted mean:

### Raw data

mw<-mean(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

mw

s.mw<-sd(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

s.mw

As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a mean is the value of the mean plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size:

round(c(mw,lb,ub))

text:
In this exercise, we will be comparing the mean gross weekly earnings (GRSSWK) and their confidence intervals using weighted and unweighted estimates. As previously, we will be using the weighting variable specifically designed for weights: PIWT24.
First, let’s examine the gross weekly earnings and compute unweighted estimates of gross weeyly earnings

summary(lfs_od24$GRSSWK)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   -9.0    -9.0    -9.0    75.8    -9.0 23076.0 

summary(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0])

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    5.0   413.2   615.0   732.5   923.0 23076.0 

hist(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],xlab = "Gross weekly earnings (GBP)")







mw<-mean(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)
mw

[1] 732.4975


Let’s now compute the confidence interval. We need to do it by hand, using the standard deviation sd() function.

s.mw<-sd(lfs_od24$GRSSWK[lfs_od24$GRSSWK>=0],na.rm=T)

s.mw

[1] 623.6522


As a reminder, the 95% confidence interval of a (point) estimate of a mean is this value plus or minus 1.96 times its standard error. The standard error itself is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size:

lb<-mw-1.96*(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))
ub<-mw+1.96*(s.mw/sqrt(nrow(lfs_od24)))

round(c(mw,lb,ub))

[1] 732 728 737


We can now say that on the basis of unweighted sample values, we could be 95% confident that the mean Gross Weekly earnings of the UK population overall range between £728 and £737 per week, that is an interval of £9.
Let’s now look at the weighted estimates. We will be using the same survey data specific functions as before.

### Let's declare our data to be survey data with PIWT as weight. 
dataex4.s<-as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24,dataex4)
 
### ... Then get the weights 
mw.s<-dataex4.s|>summarise(survey_mean(GRSSWK,vartype = "ci"))


QuestionsAnswers



What is the interval values we can be sure 95% of the value can be found, once we take weights into account?
How wide is the weighted confidence interval?
What is the effect of weighting data on the precision of estiamtes




It is between £682 and £706 per week
£24
The confidence intervals of weighted value tends to be wider than that of unweighted estimates, which makes them at the same time more representative but less precise than unweighted ones.
